newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms shrug off possible Taiwan boycott.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms shrug off possible Taiwan boycott.

text.p: Major Japanese companies in the electrical and steel industries said on Friday they were not worried about a possible boycott of Japanese products in Taiwan amid a sovereignty dispute over a chain of East China Sea islands.

Legislators of Taiwan's biggest county voted on Thursday to exclude Japanese firms from local contracts to protest Japan's assertion of sovereignty over a chain of islands in the East China Sea which are also claimed by Taiwan and China.
The Taipei County resolution also called on the county to boycott all Japanese goods.
A spokesman for Kawasaki Steel Corp said on Friday: "We have not heard that the developments at least up to now have any effect on our business there."

A spokesman for Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd said he did not see any problem. On Wednesday, Matsushita president Yoichi Morishita, asked if there would be an impact on business, told a news conference: "I don't think so."

Meanwhile, the influential Federation of Economic Organisations (Keidanren) does not have any plan at the moment to ask the Japanese government to take measures to calm the row, the federation's spokesman said.
However, some analysts said the possible escalation of the dispute could pose a serious concern for Japanese companies' Asian operations, prompting investors in the stock market to sell.
"Rather than the tension in the Middle East (U.S.-Iraq conflict), there is more concern over the dispute over the Senkaku Islands," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities.

"The market hasn't reached the stage where it is worrying if the dispute is going to evolve, if it evolves, into a buy situation or a sell situation. But psychologically, it is not a positive factor for the stock market."

The long-dormant dispute over the islands, called Senkakus in Japanese and Diaoyus in Chinese, revived in July after a Japanese right-wing group build a lighthouse on one of the islands, angering other claimants.
Nevertheless, a top government official said on Friday that Tokyo had no plans to compromise with the rival claimants.
The Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama said the government does not have the authority to bar right-wingers from erecting a lighthouse on the disputed island.
"The government does not have the authority or power to block private citizens from activities on privately owned property," he said.
